In the town of Vladimir lived a young merchant named Ivan Dmitrich Aksionov, who had two shops and a house of his own. <break time="0.8s" /> He was a handsome man with fair, curly hair, and he was full of fun and very fond of singing. <break time="0.8s" /> As a young man he had sometimes drunk too much, but after his marriage he gave it up, except now and then. <break time="0.8s" /> One summer, as he was setting off for the great fair at Nizhny, his wife said, Ivan Dmitrich, do not start today. <break time="0.8s" /> I had a bad dream about you, she went on, and in it you came home with hair that was quite gray. <break time="0.8s" /> Aksionov only laughed and said that it was a lucky sign, and he promised to bring presents home from the fair. <break time="0.8s" /> Halfway there he met a merchant he knew, and the two men had tea together and slept in neighboring rooms at an inn. <break time="0.8s" /> Aksionov did not like to sleep late, so he woke his driver before dawn and set off while the air was still cool. <break time="0.8s" /> About twenty five miles on, he stopped at another inn to feed the horses, and sitting on the porch, he began to play his guitar.

Just then a troika drove up with ringing bells, and out of it stepped an official, who at once began to question Aksionov. <break time="0.8s" /> Aksionov answered all his questions and even invited him to have tea, but the official went on asking where he had spent the night. <break time="0.8s" /> The official also wanted to know whether he had seen the merchant that morning and why he had left the inn before dawn. <break time="0.8s" /> I am the police officer of this district, he said, and the merchant with whom you spent last night has been found killed. <break time="0.8s" /> Then the two soldiers with him searched Aksionovs things, and out of a bag the officer drew a knife, crying, Whose knife is this. <break time="0.8s" /> There was blood on the knife, and Aksionov, so frightened that he could hardly speak, only stammered, It is not mine. <break time="0.8s" /> The house was locked from the inside, so you are the only person who could have done it, the officer said. <break time="0.8s" /> Aksionov swore that he was innocent, but his voice shook and his face went pale, as if he were guilty. <break time="0.8s" /> The soldiers tied his feet, threw him into the cart, and took him to the nearest town, where he was put in prison.

바로 그때. <break time="0.8s" /> 트로이카가 방울을 울리며 다가왔다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 거기서 관리 한 사람이 내렸다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그는 곧바로 악쇼노프를 심문하기 시작했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 악쇼노프는 그의 질문에 모두 대답했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 차를 마시자고 권하기까지 했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 하지만 관리는 계속 물었다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그가 어디서 밤을 보냈는지. <break time="0.8s" /> 관리는 또 알고 싶어 했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그가 그날 아침 그 상인을 보았는지. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 왜 동트기 전에 여관을 떠났는지. <break time="0.8s" /> 나는 이 지역의 경찰관이오. <break time="0.8s" /> 그가 말했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 그 상인이. <break time="0.8s" /> 당신과 함께 어젯밤을 보낸. <break time="0.8s" /> 살해된 채 발견되었소. <break time="0.8s" /> 그러자 그와 함께 온 병사 두 명이. <break time="0.8s" /> 악쇼노프의 짐을 뒤졌다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 가방 속에서. <break time="0.8s" /> 경찰관이 칼 한 자루를 꺼냈다. <break time="0.8s" /> 이건 누구 칼이오, 하고 외치며. <break time="0.8s" /> 칼에는 피가 묻어 있었다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 악쇼노프는. <break time="0.8s" /> 너무 겁에 질려 말을 거의 할 수 없었다. <break time="0.8s" /> 제 것이 아닙니다, 하고 더듬거릴 뿐이었다. <break time="0.8s" /> 집은 안에서 잠겨 있었소. <break time="0.8s" /> 그러니 당신이 유일한 사람이오. <break time="0.8s" /> 그 일을 저지를 수 있었던. <break time="0.8s" /> 경찰관이 말했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 악쇼노프는 맹세했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 자신이 결백하다고. <break time="0.8s" /> 하지만 목소리는 떨렸다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 얼굴은 창백해졌다. <break time="0.8s" /> 마치 죄를 지은 사람처럼. <break time="0.8s" /> 병사들은 그의 발을 묶었다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그를 마차에 던져 넣었다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 가장 가까운 도시로 데려갔다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그곳에서 그는 감옥에 갇혔다.

His wife. <break time="0.8s" /> Who was in despair. <break time="0.8s" /> Came to the prison. <break time="0.8s" /> With their small children. <break time="0.8s" /> And when she saw him. <break time="0.8s" /> In chains among criminals. <break time="0.8s" /> She fainted. <break time="0.8s" /> She told him. <break time="0.8s" /> That her petition to the Czar had been refused. <break time="0.8s" /> And she reminded him sadly. <break time="0.8s" /> Of her dream about his gray hair. <break time="0.8s" /> Then running her fingers through his hair. <break time="0.8s" /> She said. <break time="0.8s" /> Vanya dearest, tell your wife the truth. <break time="0.8s" /> Was it not you who did it. <break time="0.8s" /> So you, too, suspect me. <break time="0.8s" /> Cried Aksionov. <break time="0.8s" /> And hiding his face in his hands. <break time="0.8s" /> He began to weep. <break time="0.8s" /> When his family had gone for the last time. <break time="0.8s" /> He thought. <break time="0.8s" /> Only God can know the truth. <break time="0.8s" /> And only from Him can I expect mercy. <break time="0.8s" /> He wrote no more petitions. <break time="0.8s" /> And only prayed to God. <break time="0.8s" /> And he was later whipped. <break time="0.8s" /> And sent to Siberia. <break time="0.8s" /> With other prisoners. <break time="0.8s" /> Twenty six years passed in Siberia. <break time="0.8s" /> His hair turning as white as snow. <break time="0.8s" /> And his beard growing long, thin, and gray. <break time="0.8s" /> All his cheerfulness was gone. <break time="0.8s" /> And he walked slowly. <break time="0.8s" /> With a stooped back. <break time="0.8s" /> Spoke little. <break time="0.8s" /> Never laughed. <break time="0.8s" /> And often prayed. <break time="0.8s" /> He learned to make boots in prison. <break time="0.8s" /> And the other prisoners. <break time="0.8s" /> Who respected his gentleness. <break time="0.8s" /> Called him Grandfather and the Saint.

His wife, who was in despair, came to the prison with their small children, and when she saw him in chains among criminals, she fainted. <break time="0.8s" /> She told him that her petition to the Czar had been refused, and she reminded him sadly of her dream about his gray hair. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, running her fingers through his hair, she said, Vanya dearest, tell your wife the truth, Was it not you who did it. <break time="0.8s" /> So you, too, suspect me, cried Aksionov, and hiding his face in his hands, he began to weep. <break time="0.8s" /> When his family had gone for the last time, he thought, Only God can know the truth, and only from Him can I expect mercy. <break time="0.8s" /> He wrote no more petitions and only prayed to God, and he was later whipped and sent to Siberia with other prisoners. <break time="0.8s" /> Twenty six years passed in Siberia, his hair turning as white as snow and his beard growing long, thin, and gray. <break time="0.8s" /> All his cheerfulness was gone, and he walked slowly with a stooped back, spoke little, never laughed, and often prayed. <break time="0.8s" /> He learned to make boots in prison, and the other prisoners, who respected his gentleness, called him Grandfather and the Saint.
